opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that stands out most to me is generalization. These models generalize dramatically worse than people do, and it's quite obvious once you notice it.

You see it in a very concrete way. You take a model that does incredibly well on the evals, really hard competition problems, and then you use it for something real and it does something strange. You ask it to fix a bug, it introduces a second bug. You point that out, it says "you're absolutely right," and brings the first bug back. How can both be true at once? How can something be so capable on the benchmark and then make these basic mistakes?

I think part of the explanation is that we train on environments that look a lot like the evals, sometimes without intending to. So you get something like a student who practiced ten thousand hours for competitive programming. They memorized every technique, every trick, and they're the best in that domain. Then there's another student who practiced for a hundred hours, did reasonably well, and moved on. Which one will have the better career? Probably the second one. They have something that lets them learn quickly and carry it into new situations. The models are much more like the first student, and even more so.

Then there's the sample efficiency side. A teenager learns to drive in maybe ten hours, with no specific reward function. They have a robust sense of whether they're doing well or badly, something like a value function, which is probably closely tied to emotions. They can learn continually from very little data and correct themselves. Our models need enormous amounts of data, and the result still isn't as robust.

So to me the fundamental question is: what is the machine learning principle that would give you that kind of generalization? I believe it exists. I don't think evolution gave humans some magic prior for coding or mathematics, because those are too recent. So whatever humans have is something more general, and I think finding it is the central open problem.

r001.rationale: The response identifies generalization as the standout limitation and explicitly says these models generalize dramatically worse than people.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most fundamental limitation is that these models generalize much worse than people do. That's the thing. Everything else is downstream of it.

Here's what I mean. A teenager learns to drive in maybe ten hours. They've never been in that situation before, they have very little data, and yet they get it, and more importantly they know when they don't get it. They have a sense of the edge of their own competence. Our models, by contrast, consume essentially the entire internet, and then you take them slightly outside the distribution and they fail in ways that would be very strange for a person. They'll solve a hard competition math problem and then make an error that no student who could solve that problem would ever make. That mismatch is telling you something.

And I think it connects to a second thing, which is that the models' evaluations and their real usefulness have come apart. The benchmarks keep going up, and people are, I would say, somewhat underwhelmed by the economic impact relative to the numbers. Part of that is that reinforcement learning on tasks that are easy to grade teaches the model to be very good at exactly those tasks. It gets a kind of narrow competence that looks broad on paper. A person who is good at one thing tends to carry some judgment over to adjacent things. The model carries much less.

So what's missing? I don't think it's just scale, although scale continues to help. I think there is something about how humans learn that we haven't reproduced. We have a value function, in some sense, that is quite good. We feel when something is off before we can articulate it. We learn from very few samples, we learn continually, and we have a robustness that, you know, when we look at it, you'd think it would be the easy part and it turns out to be the hard part.

The pre-training era was special because the data was given to you. You didn't have to decide what to learn, you just learned everything. Now that we're running out of that kind of free lunch, the question becomes a research question again, which honestly I find exciting. It's the question of what the right learning principle actually is, such that a system can go out into the world, encounter things it hasn't seen, and handle them the way a thoughtful person would. Until we have that, you'll keep seeing this pattern where the models are extremely impressive and also, somehow, not quite there.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls current models’ much worse generalization than people their most fundamental limitation.

astra-6.text:
I think the most fundamental limitation is generalization. These models can do remarkably well on some very difficult tasks, and then fail on something that seems much simpler when the situation is a little different from what they encountered during training.

Compare that with a human. A person can learn something from a small number of examples and then apply it in a new setting. Not perfectly, of course, but with a kind of robustness that our models still lack.

So the question is: what allows you to learn something and really use it under different circumstances? We have made enormous progress, but I think there is still something important to understand there.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the most fundamental limitation and contrasts models’ failures under slight changes with humans’ ability to learn from few examples and apply knowledge in new settings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one fundamental limitation is that these models still generalize differently from people. A person can encounter a new situation, learn something from a small amount of experience, and then apply it quite reliably. With our models, you can have extraordinary performance on very difficult tasks, and then a surprisingly basic failure when the situation changes slightly.

So the question is: what is missing? Is it something about how we train them? Is it that they need to learn more directly from interacting with the world? I don’t think we should assume we know the answer. But the gap between being very capable and being reliably capable seems fundamental.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts people’s reliable transfer from limited experience to new situations with models’ basic failures after slight changes, identifying weaker generalization as a fundamental limitation.
